In summary, our research is concerned with

the following: (1) the prevalence of dyslipidaemia and hypertension; (2) the prevalence of diabetes and the co-existence of dyslipidaemias, hypertension and diabetes; (3) the prevalence of obesity; (4) the prevalence of cardiovascular disease and the co-existance of dyslipidaemic and hypertensive patients with cardiovascular disease; (5) the prevalence of stroke and the co-existant of dyslipidaemics and hypertensives with stroke.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

patients who are on both hypertension and dyslipidemia medication are likely to remain on treatment longer, and are more likely to reach their treatment target than patients who are on only one medication, but that the majority of patients in both categories do not remain on treatment long enough to reach their treatment targets, and that diabetic patients have a poorer prognosis in terms of treatment discontinuation, and a better prognosis in terms of reaching cholesterol targets.
there is no evidence to support the use of the combination drug in the management of hypertension and dyslipidemia in the general population.

the use of antihypertensives and lipid-lowering drugs in patients with hypertension or dyslipidemia, or both, is associated with a significant decrease in the risk of cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality, but not with a significant decrease of the risk of stroke.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the patients with hypertension and hyperlipidaemia were less likely to stop their treatment and they were also more likely to achieve the target values of their blood pressure and cholesterol than the patients who were treated only for hypertension or only for dyslipidaemia.
the patients with hypertension and/or dyslipidemia are not receiving the appropriate therapy to reach the target blood pressure or cholesterol level.
there is an unmet need for the initiation and maintenance of lipid-lowering therapy for hypertension and dyslipidemia in patients with hypertension.
The main takeaway from our work is that
patients with hypertension, dyslipidemia or both are at high risk of medication discontinuation, and that the risk is even higher in diabetic patients.
there are large gaps in the management of patients with hypertension and/or dyslipidaemia and that the majority of patients are not achieving treatment targets.
there is a large need for more aggressive treatment and more aggressive adherence to treatment in order to achieve treatment targets.
